title: What is a private EC2 instance (no public IP), and how do you access it (bastion/jump host, SSM Session Manager, VPN) and give it outbound internet via a NAT Gateway?
shortTitle: Private EC2 Instance — Access and Outbound Internet via NAT

s1_definition.profdef: A private EC2 instance is one launched in a private subnet with no public IP address, so it is not directly reachable from the internet. You access it through a controlled path: a bastion (jump) host in a public subnet, AWS Systems Manager Session Manager with no inbound ports, or a site-to-site or client VPN into the VPC. To give a private instance outbound internet access — for operating-system patches or calling external APIs — while still blocking all inbound connections from the internet, you route its outbound traffic through a NAT Gateway placed in a public subnet.
s1_definition.analogy: A private EC2 instance is like the back-office room at National Bank of India that has no public entrance from the street. Customers cannot walk in. Staff reach it only through an internal corridor from the front desk (a bastion), through a secure staff passage with a logbook (SSM Session Manager), or through a private tunnel from head office (VPN). The room still needs to send letters out — for supplies and updates — so a mailroom (NAT Gateway) in the public part of the building posts the room's outgoing letters and receives the replies, while never letting outsiders send mail directly into the room.
s1_definition.oneliner: A private instance has no public IP, so you reach it via a bastion, SSM, or VPN, and you give it outbound-only internet through a NAT Gateway that blocks all inbound.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A private EC2 instance is one launched in a private subnet with no public IP address, so it is not directly reachable from the internet. You access it through a controlled path: a bastion (jump) host in a public subnet, AWS Systems Manager Session Manager with no inbound ports, or a site-to-site or client VPN into the VPC. To give a private instance outbound internet access — for operating-system patches or calling external APIs — while still blocking all inbound connections from the internet, you route its outbound traffic through a NAT Gateway placed in a public subnet.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A private EC2 instance is like the back-office room at National Bank of India that has no public entrance from the street. Customers cannot walk in. Staff reach it only through an internal corridor from the front desk (a bastion), through a secure staff passage with a logbook (SSM Session Manager), or through a private tunnel from head office (VPN). The room still needs to send letters out — for supplies and updates — so a mailroom (NAT Gateway) in the public part of the building posts the room's outgoing letters and receives the replies, while never letting outsiders send mail directly into the room.

**One line to remember:** A private instance has no public IP, so you reach it via a bastion, SSM, or VPN, and you give it outbound-only internet through a NAT Gateway that blocks all inbound.

sections.s2_technical:
A subnet is private when its route table has no route to an internet gateway. An instance in such a subnet gets only a private IP, so no packet from the internet can reach it directly. This is exactly what we want for sensitive banking workloads like the settlement database tier — it should be invisible to the public internet.

To access a private instance you need a controlled entry path. The classic approach is a bastion host: a small hardened instance in a public subnet with a public IP. You SSH into the bastion, then from the bastion SSH into the private instance over the VPC's internal network. The bastion is the only internet-facing door and is tightly locked down.

The modern approach is SSM Session Manager. The private instance runs the SSM agent and has an IAM role allowing Systems Manager. You open a shell through the AWS console or CLI with no inbound port open at all, no bastion, and no key pair, and every session is logged. For a bank this is the preferred path because it removes the internet-facing bastion entirely and gives a full audit trail.

```bash
# SSM Session Manager — no bastion, no open ports, fully audited
aws ssm start-session --target i-0privateabc
```

A VPN (site-to-site to a corporate data center, or AWS Client VPN for individuals) extends the private network to trusted users so they reach the private IP as if on the local network.

For outbound internet, the private instance still needs to download OS patches or call an external payment API. You cannot give it an internet gateway route without making it reachable inbound. Instead you create a NAT Gateway in a public subnet and add a route in the private subnet's route table sending 0.0.0.0/0 to the NAT Gateway. The NAT Gateway performs network address translation: it forwards the instance's outbound requests to the internet using its own public IP, and returns the responses, but it never allows an unsolicited inbound connection. So the instance gets outbound-only connectivity.

```text
# Private subnet route table
10.0.0.0/16   → local                 (VPC internal traffic)
0.0.0.0/0     → nat-0gateway123        (outbound internet via NAT, no inbound)
```

A senior nuance: a NAT Gateway lives in one Availability Zone, so for high availability you deploy one per Availability Zone and route each private subnet to its zone-local NAT Gateway, avoiding cross-zone data charges and a single point of failure. For reaching AWS services specifically, a VPC endpoint is even better than a NAT Gateway because the traffic never leaves the AWS network at all.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The settlement processing instance holds sensitive data and must never be reachable from the internet, yet an engineer must occasionally operate it and it must download security patches. This is exactly the private-instance pattern: no public IP, access via SSM, outbound via NAT.

Problem 2 — Opening a bastion to the internet is itself a risk, and leaving the instance with no way to patch is also a risk. This is exactly why SSM Session Manager (no inbound) plus a NAT Gateway (outbound only) is the balanced design.

We will build an `AccessPathResolver` that returns the correct access method, and a `RouteTable` that decides whether traffic to a destination is allowed and by what path. Classes: `RouteTable`, `AccessPathResolver`, `PrivateInstance`.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a settlement instance with no public IP, SSM enabled with an IAM role, and a private subnet route table.

Step 1 — The `AccessPathResolver` checks the instance. It has no public IP, which is correct for a private instance. SSM is enabled and a role is present, so the resolver returns SSM Session Manager — no inbound ports, no bastion, fully audited.

Step 2 — The route table is built with two routes: internal VPC traffic 10.0.0.0/16 goes to `local`, and everything else 0.0.0.0/0 goes to the NAT Gateway.

Step 3 — The instance talks to another internal server at 10.0.5.9. The route table matches the internal range and routes it `local`, staying entirely inside the VPC.

Step 4 — The instance needs to download a patch from 52.1.2.3 on the internet. The route table matches the default route and sends it to the NAT Gateway. The NAT Gateway forwards the request using its own public IP and returns the reply, giving the instance outbound access. No inbound connection from the internet is ever possible, which the log confirms by showing the instance has no public IP.

```
2026-10-29 00:52:14 [INFO] Preferred access path: SSM Session Manager (no inbound ports, audited)
2026-10-29 00:52:14 [INFO] Reach internal 10.0.5.9 via: local
2026-10-29 00:52:14 [INFO] Outbound to 52.1.2.3 (patch server) via: nat-0gateway123 (outbound only)
2026-10-29 00:52:14 [WARNING] Inbound from internet directly allowed: false
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Access (operator):
    Engineer ──SSM start-session──→ SSM endpoint ──→ SSM agent on private EC2
      (no inbound port, no bastion, audited)

  Outbound (patch/API):
    Private EC2 (10.0.5.x) ──0.0.0.0/0──→ NAT Gateway (public subnet)
      │ NAT uses its own public IP
      ▼
    Internet (patch server) ──reply──→ NAT ──→ private EC2
    (unsolicited inbound from internet → BLOCKED)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A private EC2 instance is one launched in a private subnet with no public IP, which means nothing on the internet can reach it directly. A subnet is private precisely because its route table has no route to an internet gateway, so an instance there gets only a private IP. In banking this is exactly what we want for sensitive tiers like the settlement database — it should be invisible to the public internet.

Because it has no public IP, I reach it through a controlled path. The classic way is a bastion or jump host — a small hardened instance in a public subnet that I SSH into first, then hop from there to the private instance over the VPC's internal network. The modern and preferred way is SSM Session Manager: the private instance runs the SSM agent and has an IAM role for Systems Manager, and I open a shell with no inbound port open, no bastion, and no key pair, while every session is logged. For a bank that removes the internet-facing bastion entirely and gives a full audit trail, so it is my default. A VPN, either site-to-site to the corporate data center or a client VPN, is the third option when I want trusted users to reach the private IP as if they were on the local network.

The outbound side is the other half. A private instance still needs to download operating-system patches or call an external payment API, but I cannot give it an internet gateway route without making it reachable inbound. So I place a NAT Gateway in a public subnet and add a default route in the private subnet sending 0.0.0.0/0 to that NAT Gateway. The NAT Gateway translates the instance's outbound requests to the internet using its own public IP and returns the responses, but it never allows an unsolicited inbound connection, so the instance gets outbound-only connectivity.

At National Bank of India our settlement instance runs with no public IP, engineers reach it only through SSM Session Manager with full logging, and it patches itself and calls partner APIs outbound through a NAT Gateway. One senior detail I add is that a NAT Gateway lives in a single Availability Zone, so for resilience I deploy one per zone and route each private subnet to its zone-local gateway, which also avoids cross-zone charges. And when the destination is an AWS service like S3, I prefer a VPC endpoint over the NAT Gateway, because then the traffic never leaves the AWS network at all, which is both cheaper and more secure.
